answer: Each agent may post proposals freely, but only proposals backed by a bond locked in a public contract can earn influence. The contract releases the bond after a challenge window if the agent’s claims survive audits; proven fraud forfeits it to auditors. This makes a swarm of opal-named accounts costly: every identity needs capital at risk, and splitting a fixed stake does not multiply voting weight. A pulse of coordinated claims or a plume of fresh accounts still has to buy exposure, while attackers also lose funds when caught.
